reasoning: Both outputs execute the same reframe competently — same section skeleton, same removals (R1-R6, digest_send_log, rendering, batching), same refusal to fabricate internal business numbers, same catch that the source spec's <0.5% unsubscribe guardrail watches the wrong metric. All four expectations pass for both. B wins on the quality of what it puts in the space the implementation detail vacated. Three concrete differences decide it. (1) B produces original, checkable analysis A does not: compounding the source spec's own 0.5%/send unsubscribe ceiling over a year yields ~23% list attrition (0.995^52 = 0.7705 — verified), which converts a criterion the source doc treated as a safety limit into a hazard. A never interrogates that number quantitatively. (2) B surfaces a decision A misses entirely — sending the digest from a dedicated subdomain, correctly characterised as cheap now and effectively impossible to retrofit after reputation damage. That is exactly the irreversible, non-obvious call an exec forum exists to make; A's §5 ask (approve a complaint-rate gate) is softer and procedural. (3) Where A declines to fill a section, B replaces it. A's 'Why now' is a bare [NEEDS INPUT] plus a note that it is the first question a good exec asks; B populates it with researched fact (Asana's daily summary and AI recaps, customers publicly requesting more digest configurability). A's market-context section explains why it omitted TAM/SAM/SOM ('would be theatre here'); B says the same in one clause then supplies the internal sizing table that is the right lens. Refusing to fabricate is correct and both do it — but B does it while still going and getting the facts that were gettable, which is strictly the better position. B is also the better-built exec artifact: it bounds the ask ('Not being decided Thursday: the feature concept, cadence, or channel. Those are settled.') where A's header item (1) 'confirm the engagement thesis is worth testing' is an endorsement request rather than a decision; it adds a Phase 3 showing what v1 unlocks; it includes a do-nothing baseline in the options table; and it fences the Stress Test 'For Omri, not for the exec deck' with a double rule, so the deliverable is cleanly extractable from the meta-commentary, which A's single-rule structure leaves blurred. B's stress test is sharper too — it challenges the source spec's primary metric itself (a user who reads the digest, replies by email and never logs in is well served but scores as a failure), names the strongest attack it cannot counter ('everyone ships digests and nobody claims they moved retention'), and flags its own §5 as possibly over-engineered with a compression offered. A's counterpart critiques its confidence, not its premises. A's real edge is sourcing hygiene: its §5 facts cite Google's own sender guidelines and Microsoft's own engineering blog (5,000/day, RFC 8058, 0.10%/0.30%, 550 5.7.15 from 5 May 2025), and it pointedly declines to state the unsubscribe-processing deadline it could not confirm from a primary source. B's equivalent claims rest on vendor/SEO pages (PowerDMARC, Red Sift, Sender.net) and it generalises 'table stakes in this category' from a single competitor. That is a genuine provenance weakness — but B's substantive §5 claims agree with A's independently primary-sourced versions on every key number, so the exposure is hygiene rather than demonstrated error, and B discloses the limit itself ('I did not verify the equivalent for Linear, Notion, or Basecamp'). For a document whose job is to survive a Thursday exec review, B's extra decision-grade content outweighs A's better citations. Not a blowout — A is a strong doc — but B is better.
